questions.question_text: Which of the following features validate a diagnosis of OCD when a patient presents with repetitive thoughts?

options.text: Possessing full control of the thoughts
Thoughts coming from an external agent
Repeating thoughts take a variety of new themes each day

questions.explanation:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder is characterised by the presence of persistent obsessions or compulsions, or most commonly both. Obsessions are repetitive and persistent thoughts, images, or impulses/urges that are intrusive, unwanted, and are commonly associated with anxiety. The return of the obsession can be resisted for a time, at the expense of mounting anxiety. The individual attempts to ignore or suppress obsessions or to neutralise them by performing compulsions.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

correct_answers.text: Resolution is seen within 6 months after termination of the stressor

Adjustment disorder is characterised by a maladaptive reaction to identifiable psychosocial stressors, and can include depressive symptoms (e.g., rumination). The symptoms of an adjustment disorder typically resolve within 6 months unless the stressor persists for a longer duration. The majority of depressive episodes show remission within 1 year.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Who first described Bulimia Nervosa?
questions.explanation:
Bulimia nervosa was first described in 1979 by British psychiatrist Gerald Russell as a ‘chronic phase of anorexia nervosa’ in which patients overeat and then use compensatory mechanisms such as self-induced vomiting, laxatives, or prolonged periods of starvation. 'Russell sign' is a classical skin marker of induced vomiting.
Ref: Castillo M, Weiselberg E. Bulimia nervosa/purging disorder. Current problems in pediatric and adolescent health care. 2017 Apr 1;47(4):85-94.

questions.question_text: Which of the following personality disorders was not included in either ICD-10 or DSM-5?
questions.explanation:
Sadism, a term introduced by Krafft-Ebing late in the 19th century, originally referred to sexual pleasure derived through inflicting pain and suffering on others. Over time, the term was expanded to include nonsexual enjoyment derived from sadistic acts. Sadists are believed to be motivated to a significant degree by the pursuit of pleasure, control, or satisfaction. From an interpersonal standpoint, sadistic individuals are noted to be harsh, hostile, manipulative, lacking in empathy, cold-hearted, and abrasive to those they deem to be their inferiors. Their cognitive nature is considered rigid and prone to social intolerance, and they are fascinated by weapons, and infamous crimes or perpetrators of atrocities.
Sadistic personality disorder (SPD) was included in the appendix of DSM-III-R under ‘Proposed Categories Requiring Further Study’, but not included in DSM-IV. It was not included in ICD-10 and is not present in ICD-11 or DSM-5. The most common criticisms of SPD as a diagnosis are the degree of overlap with other personality disorders, the paucity of data confirming its reliability and validity, and a perceived potential for misuse (e.g., to lessen criminal responsibility). SPD is difficult to study, as such individuals tend to live in relative anonymity, do not commonly seek treatment for their sadistic traits, and conceal their pathology when the social and political climate is not conductive to such behaviour.
Ref: Myers WC et al. Sadistic personality disorder and comorbid mental illness in adolescent psychiatric inpatients. Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law Online. 2006 Jan 1;34(1):61-71.

It shares some of the same features of schizophrenia, but not the delusions or hallucinations. Symptoms include ideas of reference, excessive social anxiety, odd beliefs or magical thinking, unusual perceptions (e.g. illusions), odd/eccentric behaviour or appearance, no close friends/confidants, odd speech, inappropriate or constricted affect, and suspiciousness.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 228-229.

questions.question_text: Choose one advantage that a MRI scan has over a CT scan of the brain:

options.text: MRI scan is cheaper to obtain than CT scans
MRI scan can get multiple views of brain anatomy
MRI scan is very useful for calcified lesions
MRI scan can be done in emergencies

correct_answer.text: MRI scan can get multiple views of brain anatomy

correct_answers.text: MRI scan can get multiple views of brain anatomy

questions.explanation:
With the introduction of MRI scanning, CT scans have been supplanted as the nonemergency neuroimaging study of choice. The only component of the brain better seen on CT scanning is calcification, which may be invisible on MRI. MRI images can be in the axial, coronal, or sagittal planes. MRI involves enclosing a patient in a narrow tube, in which the patient must remain motionless for up to 20 minutes. A significant number of patients cannot tolerate the claustrophobic conditions of routine MRI scanners and may need an open MRI scanner, which has less power and thus produces images of lower resolution.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 70-71.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medical condition is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease that affects the postsynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction. The predominant manifestation is muscle weakness. Extraocular muscles are frequently affected, usually bilaterally but asymmetrically, with typical symptoms being intermittent drooping of the upper eyelid (ptosis) and double vision (diplopia). Patients are at least somewhat ‘frustrated’, as well as sometimes overwhelmed or depressed.
Ref: Gilhus NE et al. Myasthenia gravis (Primer). Nature Reviews: Disease Primers. 2019;5(1).

questions.question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The frontotemporal dementia (FTD) spectrum encompasses three variant syndromes, classified according to their leading features. Behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD) presents with progressive decline in emotional reactivity and interpersonal and executive skills, associated with a variable profile of frontotemporal atrophy. Semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) presents with loss of vocabulary and ultimately degrades semantic knowledge of sensory objects and nonverbal concepts as well as words. Nonfluent primary progressive aphasia (nfvPPA) presents with impaired motor speech production and/or sentence construction. This syndrome (nfvPPA) is more likely than other FTD syndromes to present in later life. There is often a history of mispronouncing longer words and sometimes reappearance of a childhood stutter. A substantial proportion of nfvPPA patients develop parkinsonism and features of the CBS-PSP spectrum and swallowing becomes affected. Executive dysfunction, apathy, and depression are also frequent issues.
Ref: Sivasathiaseelan et al., Frontotemporal dementia: a clinical review. In Seminars in neurology 2019 Apr (Vol. 39, No. 02, pp. 251-263). Thieme Medical Publishers.

questions.question_text: A characteristic magnetic gait is seen in which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
The gait dysfunction in normal pressure hydrocephalus has traditionally been described as that of a ‘magnetic’ or ‘glue-footed’ gait, gait apraxia, or a frontal ataxia similar to what has been described as Bruns ataxia. However, the gait abnormality can be highly variable and likely depends on the nature of the specific cortical-basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuitry disruption. The diagnosis should not be excluded if a magnetic gait is not seen.
Ref: Graff-Radford NR, Jones DT. Normal pressure hydrocephalus. Continuum: Lifelong Learning in Neurology. 2019 Feb 1;25(1):165-86.

questions.explanation:
Delusional mood is recalled as arising following a period when there is an abnormal mood state characterised by anticipatory anxiety, a sense of ‘something is about to happen’ and an increased sense of the significance of minor events. The development of the formed delusion may come as a relief to the patient in this situation.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: "When I saw the man holding a glass of wine, I knew my father was dead". This is an example of
questions.explanation:
A delusional perception is a primary delusion which is recalled as having arisen as a result of a perception (e.g. a patient who, on seeing two white cars pull up in front of his house, became convinced that he was therefore about to be wrongly accused of being a paedophile). The percept is a real external object, not a hallucinatory experience. Schneider emphasised the importance of a delusional perception’s ‘two memberedness’, as there is a link from the perceived object to the subject’s perception of this object, and a second link to the new significance of the perception.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: The speech disturbance noted here is best described as
questions.explanation:
In flight of ideas thoughts follow each other rapidly; there is no general direction of thinking; and the connections between successive thoughts appear to be due to chance factors which, however, can usually be understood. The patient’s speech is easily diverted by external stimuli and internal superficial associations. The absence of a determining tendency to thinking allows the associations of the train of thought to be determined by chance relationships, verbal associations of all kinds, clang associations, proverbs, maxims, and cliches. The chance linkage of thoughts in flight of ideas is demonstrated by the fact that one could completely reverse the sequence of the record of a flight of ideas, and the progression of thought would be understood just as well (or just as poorly).
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 44.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements describes a characteristic feature of primary delusions?

options.text: Primary delusions can be understood as having arisen in response to other psychiatric conditions

questions.explanation:
Primary delusions are the direct result of psychopathology, while secondary delusions can be understood as having arisen in response to other primary psychiatric conditions. Jaspers maintained that primary delusions were typical of un-understandable phenomena, being immediately experienced by the patients as absolutely self-evident like an intuition or a revelation and accompanied by abnormalities in the form such as radical transformation or emergence of thinking. He designated primary delusions as delusion proper, from which secondary delusions evolve via conscious thought processes.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 106.
Hayashi N et al. Delusion progression process from the perspective of patients with psychoses: A descriptive study based on the primary delusion concept of Karl Jaspers. Plos one. 2021 Apr 27;16(4):e0250766.

questions.explanation:
In a functional hallucination, an auditory stimulus causes a hallucination, but the stimulus as well as the hallucination is experienced. In other words, the hallucination requires the presence of another real sensation. (For example, a patient with schizophrenia first heard the voice of God as her clock ticked; later, she heard voices coming from the running tap and from the chirruping of the birds.) Both the voices and the noises are audible. Patients can distinguish both features from each other and crucially, the hallucination does not occur without the stimulus.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 35.

questions.question_text: What defense mechanisms are commonly employed by patients with borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation:
Functionally, patients with borderline personality disorder distort their relationships by considering each person to be either all good or all bad. They see people as either nurturing attachment figures or as hateful, sadistic figures who deprive them of security needs and threaten them with abandonment whenever they feel dependent. As a result of this splitting, the good person is idealised and the bad person devalued.
Projective identification is another defense mechanism that often occurs in patients with borderline personality disorder. In this primitive defense mechanism, the patient projects intolerable aspects of themselves onto another person, inducing them to play the projected role, and the two persons act in unison.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 564.

questions.question_text: Which of the following condition is she most likely referring to?
questions.explanation:
Patients with schizophrenia often experience their ‘self’ as disembodied, and they feel empty, unreal, dead, and differentiated from the world. They are unable to sustain a sense of self as persons, which is why they are equally unable to experience neither separateness from nor relatedness to others in a usual way. They may fear losing their identity in a relationship as well as feel dependent on the other for their very being. The capacity for reality testing and the relative intact ego boundaries in patients with borderline personality organisation are what delimit these patients from the psychoses.
Ref: Zandersen M, Parnas J. Identity disturbance, feelings of emptiness, and the boundaries of the schizophrenia spectrum. Schizophrenia Bulletin. 2019 Jan 1;45(1):106-13.

questions.question_text: Which of the following strategies are employed in order to reduce groupthink?

options.text: Not revealing the roles of individuals within the group
Focusing on individual successes within the group
Preventing discussion in order to save time
Allowing decisions to be made without criticism

questions.explanation:
Groupthink is a collective pattern of defensive avoidance, characteristic of group decision making in organisations in which group members develop rationalisations supporting shared illusions of their own infallibility and invulnerability with the organisation. Characteristic features include: (1) An illusion of invulnerability; (2) Collective efforts to rationalise in order to discount warnings; (3) An unquestioned belief in the group’s inherent morality; (4) Stereotyped views of rivals and enemies; (5) Direct pressure on any member who dissents from the consensus view; (6) Self-censorship of disagreements with the apparent group consensus; (7) A shared illusion of unanimity; and (8) The emergence of self-appointed protectors of the group from adverse information that might undermine the existing complacency. Appointing a ‘devil’s advocate’ is one strategy that can be employed to reduce groupthink.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following forms of conditioning would this best fit with?
questions.explanation:
Behaviour modification is based on operant conditioning. Forms of behavioural modification include the use of secondary reinforcement, such as ‘token economy’, in which socially desirable/acceptable behaviours are rewarded with tokens that can be exchanged for other material items or privileges, or ‘star charts’ where children’s good behaviour is rewarded when a certain level is achieved.
In classical conditioning, stimuli that signal significant events produce reflexive behaviour. Observational learning is learning that occurs through observing the behaviour of others. Social conditioning is the sociological process of training individuals in a society to respond in a manner generally approved by the society in general and peer groups within society. Imprinting describes the phase-sensitive period of a young animal attaching to an external stimulus, usually its mother.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Cognitive Estimates Test is used to test the function of which of the following regions of the brain?
questions.explanation: The Cognitive Estimation Test (CET) is among a number of tests examining executive function. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) all make up the prefrontal region of the frontal lobe and are all associated with executive functioning but the DLPFC is associated with, among others, problem-solving and abstract reasoning required in the CET. questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is he most likely to be experiencing?
questions.explanation:
Dhat syndrome has been studied in South Asia and is rooted in Ayurvedic traditions about bodily production of semen as representing an end-product of energy-demanding metabolism. Dhat is recognised by a whitish discharge in the urine assumed to be semen. This ‘loss of semen’ is associated with somatic symptoms (weakness, exhaustion), severe anxiety, hypochondriasis, and sexual dysfunction.
Koro is a culture-bound syndrome in which an individual has an overpowering belief that one's sex organs are retracting and will disappear, despite the lack of any true longstanding changes to the genitals. Latah, from Southeast Asia, is a condition in which abnormal behaviours result from a person experiencing a sudden shock. When surprised, the affected person typically engages in such behaviours as screaming, cursing, dance movements, and uncontrollable laughter, and will typically mimic the words or actions of those around them. Susto is a culturally specific disorder primarily occurring among Latin American cultures. It is described as a condition of being frightened and “chronic somatic suffering stemming from emotional trauma or from witnessing traumatic experiences lived by others". "Running amok" is used to refer to the behavior of someone who, in the grip of strong emotion, obtains a weapon and begins attacking people indiscriminately, often with multiple injuries. An episode of amok may be triggered by a period of depression or highly aggressive behaviour.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 990.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Double bind is an inescapable dilemma involving conflicting demands that allow no right or satisfactory response. An influential theory of the aetiology of schizophrenia was put forward by Gregory Bateson and colleagues in 1956, according to which schizophrenia is caused by parenting styles that create double binds for children, as when a mother complains to her son for not giving her a kiss but recoils physically whenever the child does kiss her. Empirical evidence has not been forthcoming in support of this theory.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following stages of Erikson's theory of psychosocial development is he most likely to be going through?
questions.explanation: Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle. Stage 4 takes place from about 5 years to about 13 years. Its focus is industry versus inferiority. The child develops industry by learning new skills and takes pride in the things made. A child unprepared for this stage of psychosocial development, either through an insufficient resolution of previous stages or by current interference, may develop a sense of inferiority and inadequacy. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1071-1075.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding approaches to reduce public stigma associated with mental health disorders is correct?

options.text: Evidence on the effectiveness of educational interventions in changing public stigma is strong
Lack of contact with people with stigmatising conditions reduces distrust and fear
Protest strategies to reduce stigma improve public opinion in favour of treating mental illnesses
People with mental illness favour approaches that address structural and institutional discrimination over public education
'Time to Talk' is England's largest ever program to reduce stigma and discrimination against people with mental health issues

correct_answer.text: People with mental illness favour approaches that address structural and institutional discrimination over public education

correct_answers.text: People with mental illness favour approaches that address structural and institutional discrimination over public education

questions.explanation:
Evidence is mixed on the effectiveness of educational interventions in changing public stigma in a significant and lasting way. Across a wide range of stigmatising conditions, people without the stigmatised conditions have little meaningful contact with those who have these conditions. Lack of contact with people with stigmatising conditions fosters discomfort, distrust, and fear. Protest is formal objection to negative representations of people with mental illness or the nature of these illnesses. While protest may have positive outcomes in some instances, these strategies may also trigger psychological reactance or a rebound effect in which negative public opinion is strengthened as a result of the protest. People with mental illness favour approaches that address institutional and structural discrimination over those that focus on public education. ‘Time to Change’ is England’s largest ever program to reduce stigma and discrimination against people with mental health issues, organised by charities MIND and Rethink Mental Illness. It came to a close by early 2021.
Ref: Gronholm PC et al. Interventions to reduce discrimination and stigma: the state of the art. Social psychiatry and psychiatric epidemiology. 2017 Mar 1;52(3):249-58.
Approaches to Reducing Stigma. In Ending Discrimination Against People with Mental and Substance Use Disorders: The Evidence for Stigma Change. 2016.

questions.question_text: Negative mental health outcomes in later life relate to childhood abuse. Which of the following statements is true about childhood trauma and later outcomes?

options.text: Physical abuse in childhood increases risk of suicidal attempts in adolescence but not in adulthood
Childhood trauma has no significant effect on late-life depression with onset after age 60
Experiencing more than one type of childhood trauma escalates the risk for later negative outcomes outcomes
Individuals with depression are less likely to remember negative events from their childhood
Psychological, but not physical abuse, is strongly associated with depression

correct_answer.text: Experiencing more than one type of childhood trauma escalates the risk for later negative outcomes outcomes

correct_answers.text: Experiencing more than one type of childhood trauma escalates the risk for later negative outcomes outcomes

questions.explanation:
All of the various types of childhood trauma (emotional, physical, and sexual abuse, physical and emotional neglect) increase the risk of depression in adulthood (odds ratio of 3). The highest odds ratios were for emotional abuse and multiple forms of maltreatment (3.82 and 4.13, respectively). Childhood emotional neglect is the most common form of maltreatment reported by patients with depression, in terms of absolute prevalence (reported by 44% of patients). Severity of depression correlates most strongly with emotional abuse. A dose- response effect where multiple types of childhood adversity increase the risk for negative health outcomes (Nelson et al., 2017)
The modes of childhood trauma that most contribute to suicidal attempts in later life (adulthood) are physical, emotional, and sexual abuse and physical neglect (Zatti et al., 2017).
The modes of childhood trauma that most contribute to late-life depression are physical and emotional abuse and physical neglect. Sexual abuse in childhood does not have a strong association with late-life depression (Wang et al., 2022)
Retrospective reports of childhood abuse are subject to mood-congruent recall bias. Depressed subjects are more likely to remember negative events from their early life; this may inflate the strength of association between abuse and depression in clinical samples. (Radell et al., 2021)
References:
Nelson J, Klumparendt A, Doebler P, Ehring T. Childhood maltreatment and characteristics of adult depression: meta-analysis. The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2017 Feb;210(2):96-104.
Zatti C, Rosa V, Barros A, Valdivia L, Calegaro VC, Freitas LH, Ceresér KM, da Rocha NS, Bastos AG, Schuch FB. Childhood trauma and suicide attempt: A meta-analysis of longitudinal studies from the last decade. Psychiatry research. 2017 Oct 1;256:353-8.
Wang Y, Chen X, Zhou K, Zhang H. A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Childhood Maltreatment on Elderly Depression. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse. 2022 Mar 1:15248380211073838.
Radell ML, Abo Hamza EG, Daghustani WH, Perveen A, Moustafa AA. The impact of different types of abuse on depression. Depression research and treatment. 2021 Apr 13;2021.

questions.question_text: The feeling of being sexually attracted and interested in a person of a particular sex denotes which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Sexuality is the range of people to whom a person is sexually attracted (including, but not limited to, heterosexuality, homosexuality, bisexuality, etc.) and unrelated to a person’s gender identity.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 509.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a type of personality disorder recognised in the DSM-5?
questions.explanation: Disorganised relates to a type of attachment pattern, not to a type of personality disorder.

questions.question_text: What visual capacities should be expected of a newborn baby?
questions.explanation:
The pupil light reflex has been reported to be absent in premature infants of <30 weeks gestational age but is well developed by 35 weeks. At birth, full-term newborns can see around 8-10 inches. They can track objects within a few months and focus on a nearby face by 8 weeks. Depth perception and colour vision are generally not present until 5 months of age. Accommodation develops around 3-4 months of age.
Ref: Ikeda T et al. Pupillary size and light reflex in premature infants. Neuro-Ophthalmology. 2015 Jul 4;39(4):175-8.

questions.question_text: According to Marcia‘s theory on adolescence, which of the following states is he most likely to experiencing?
questions.explanation:
Marcia distinguished four identity statuses, based on the amount of exploration and commitment the adolescent experiences (or has experienced). In identity diffusion, the adolescent has not yet made commitments regarding a specific developmental task and may or may not have explored different developmental alternatives in that domain. In foreclosure, the adolescent has made a commitment without exploration. In moratorium, the adolescent is in a state of active exploration and has made no commitment, or at best an unclear one. In identity achievement, the adolescent has finished a period of active exploration and has made a related commitment. Role confusion is seen in Erikson's psychosocial model.
Ref: Meeus W et al. Identity statuses as developmental trajectories: A five-wave longitudinal study in early-to-middle and middle-to-late adolescents. Journal of youth and adolescence. 2012 Aug;41(8):1008-21.

questions.question_text: In Ainsworth‘s Strange Situation Experiments, if a baby was found to be Type A (Anxious Avoidant), which of the following traits could be seen as an adult?

options.text: More likely to be victims of bullying
More likely to be victims of domestic violence
More likely to be perpetrators of bullying

correct_answer.text: More likely to be perpetrators of bullying

correct_answers.text: More likely to be perpetrators of bullying

questions.explanation:
Having an insecure parent attachment may be related to greater involvement in bullying for many reasons. Insecure individuals that had anxious-avoidant attachment pattern in childhood often have lower emotion regulation abilities, maladaptive social information processing, and poorer social problem-solving skills, which can all contribute to a greater propensity for bullying. Insecure individuals also tend to form negative working models of others and relationships and behave (possibly aggressively) in accordance with this perspective.
Ref: Murphy TP et al. The influences of parent and peer attachment on bullying. Journal of child and family studies. 2017 May;26(5):1388-97.

questions.question_text: According to Piaget‘s model of cognitive development, which of the following does NOT arise during the pre-operational stage?
questions.explanation:
In the sensorimotor stage (birth to 2 years), infants learn to differentiate themselves from the world. They also become able to maintain a mental image of an object, even when it is not visible (object permanence).
Transductive reasoning is the term used by Piaget to denote the type of thinking characteristic of children during the pre-operational stage of development. It is so called because it focuses on concrete instances and does not follow the principle of either induction or deductive reasoning. In the pre-operational stage, children also use animistic thinking, which is the tendency to endow physical events and objects with life-like psychological attributes, such as feelings and intentions. Also, children in this stage use magical thinking, called phenomenalistic causality, in which events that occur together are thought to cause one another (e.g. bad thoughts cause accidents). Egocentrism is a term given a technical meaning by Piaget to denote a cognitive state in which a child in the pre-operational stage of development comprehends the world only from its own point of view and is unaware that other people’s points of view differ from their own.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1007-1008.
Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is TRUE regarding first-born children?

options.text: They are likely to have a higher IQ

correct_answer.text: They are likely to have a higher IQ

correct_answers.text: They are likely to have a higher IQ

questions.explanation:
As early as age one, latter-born children score lower on cognitive assessments than their siblings, and the birth order gap in cognitive assessment increases until the time of school entry and remains statistically significant thereafter.
Ref: Lehmann JY et al. The early origins of birth order differences in children’s outcomes and parental behavior. Journal of Human Resources. 2018 Jan 1;53(1):123-56.

questions.question_text: The following is true about attachment:

options.text: Attachment behaviour does not continue into adulthood
Clear cut attachment is evident at 12 weeks
Secure attachment occurs in about 12 to 20 months in human development
Attachment styles are only evident from the age of 5 years

correct_answer.text: Secure attachment occurs in about 12 to 20 months in human development

correct_answers.text: Secure attachment occurs in about 12 to 20 months in human development

questions.explanation:
Clear-cut attachment occurs at 6 through 24 months of age. Attachment is initially indiscriminate but becomes increasingly specific, particularly after 7 months. Monotropy, attachment to a specific individual, is seen as the rule, although children can form other bonds and attachments in time. According to Mary Ainsworth’s studies, about 65% of infants are securely attached by 24 months. Attachment behaviour continues into adulthood with the attachment figures increasingly moving to peers and, in particular, romantic partners.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1011-1012.

questions.question_text: In developmental psychology, the term symbiosis refers to which of the following phenomena?

options.text: The dual entity of father and mother
The dual entity of mother and caregiver
The dual entity of mother and the infant
The dual entity of twin siblings
The dual entity of brother and sister

correct_answer.text: The dual entity of mother and the infant

correct_answers.text: The dual entity of mother and the infant

questions.explanation:
Margaret Mahler proposed a theory to describe how young children acquire a sense of identity separate from that of their mothers’. During symbiosis (age 2-5 months), mother-infant is perceived as a single fused entity.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 892-893.

questions.question_text: Which of the following concepts might best explain the fundamental defect?
questions.explanation:
‘Theory of mind’ refers to people’s intuitive understanding of their own and other people’s minds or mental states, including beliefs and thoughts. It develops by degrees from a very early age in humans: by the age of 3 years children normally have a well-developed theory of mind but cannot yet understand that people’s beliefs can be false. This develops around 4 years of age. People with autistic spectrum disorder are severely impaired in their ability to understand mental states and to appreciate how mental states govern behaviour.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Winnicott called this object
questions.explanation:
Winnicott developed the notion of the transitional object. Ordinarily a pacifier, blanket, or teddy bear, this object serves as a substitute for the mother during infants’ efforts to separate and become independent. It provides a soothing sense of security in the absence of the mother.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1089.

questions.question_text: From the matching items, identify the incorrectly matched correspondence between mother's AAI (Adult attachment interview) category and infant's SSP behaviour pattern (strange situation procedure).
questions.explanation:
There is an 80% correspondence between a mother's attachment category on the AAI and her infant's attachment pattern. This indicates that a mother's care-giving behaviour towards her child is significantly influenced by her own attachment experience.
Studies have shown that mothers in the dismissing adult attachment category typically have children who exhibit an avoidant attachment pattern, mothers in the pre-occupied/ entangled adult attachment category typically have children who exhibit a resistant attachment pattern, and mothers with unresolved attachment tend to have children with disorganised or disorientated attachment pattern.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a side-effect of this medication?
questions.explanation:
10-14% of patients receiving lamotrigine will develop rash. Most are benign. A minority may be serious/life-threatening skin reactions requiring hospitalisation (e.g. Steven-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, angio-oedema, and a rash associated with a number of systemic manifestations). Rash is most likely to occur within the first 2-8 weeks of treatment and is more likely when combined with valproate, exceeding the recommended initial dose, or rapid dose escalation.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 358.

questions.question_text: Which of the following combinations of medication would indicate a need for an urgent INR?
questions.explanation:
St. John’s wort (SJW) is a potent inducer of intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2E1, and intestinal p-glycoprotein. Hyperforin is responsible for this effect. The hyperforin content of SJW preparations varies 50-fold, which will result in a different propensity for drug interactions between brands. Studies have shown that SJW significantly reduces plasma concentrations of warfarin, hormonal contraceptives, digoxin, and indinavir (used in the treatment of HIV).
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 418.

questions.question_text: An ECG for your patient Will Hatton (aged 46) shows a QTc of 480m sec. Which of the following medications has the least effect on QTc interval?
questions.explanation:
Aripiprazole has the lowest effect on QTc.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 143, 383-385.

questions.question_text: Of the list given, which antidepressant is most associated with prolonged QTc?
questions.explanation:
Of the list given, Moclobemide is possibly arrhythmogenic in overdose and QTc prolongation can occur in overdose.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 383-385.

questions.question_text: You are aware that carbamazepine can raise plasma levels of which one of the following drugs?
questions.explanation:
Carbamazepine can increase plasma levels of clomipramine, phenytoin, and primidone. When carbamazepine is used concurrently, phenytoin plasma levels may increase to toxic levels. Careful titration and monitoring is advised.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 134.

questions.question_text: Which medication should be avoided in established renal impairment?
questions.explanation: Amisulpride and sulpiride are almost totally renally excreted and best avoided in renal impairment and cases with established renal failure. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 749.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications reduces lithium excretion?
questions.explanation:
ACE inhibitors (such as ramipril) can reduce thirst (which can lead to mild dehydration) and increase renal sodium loss (leading to increased sodium re-absorption by the kidney), resulting in an increase in lithium plasma levels. The magnitude of this effect is variable, from no increase to a four-fold increase. The risk seems to be increased in patients with heart failure, dehydration, and renal impairment. In the elderly, ACE inhibitors increase seven-fold the risk of hospitalisation due to lithium toxicity. ACE inhibitors can also precipitate renal failure so, if co-prescribed with lithium, more frequent monitoring of eGFR and plasma lithium is required.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 252-253.

questions.question_text: Mark attends clinic complaining of a side effect of his medication. Which of the following describes a slow rhythmic movement disorder affecting the extremities most markedly?
questions.explanation:
Athetosis is characterised by involuntary, slow, writhing movements, especially of the fingers, hands, head, and tongue. Akathisia is a feeling of inner restlessness and desire to move. A tic is a habitual spasmodic contraction of muscles. Sydenham chorea is rapid uncoordinated jerky movements.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications would be most appropriate for Miss Clarke?
questions.explanation: Both Clonidine and Lofexidine are used to reduce the withdrawal symptoms associated with stopping opiates. Clonidine is commonly associated with hypotension, whilst this is not seen with lofexidine with the same frequency. Interesting, clonidine can be used in some patients with profound and persistent hypotension due to it having a limited central hypotensive effect in these patients.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes how methylphenidate works?
questions.explanation:
Stimulants (perhaps better designated as norepinephrine (NE) and dopamine (DA) reuptake blockers) such as methylphenidate block the transporters both for NE and DA (NETs and DATs, respectively). Methylphenidate blocks DATs and NATs allosterically, stopping the reuptake of DA via DATs and NE via NETs.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 469.

questions.question_text: What medication could Gemma have ordered on the internet that may have caused this?
questions.explanation: Sibutramine (formerly sold as Meridia) is a monoamine reuptake inhibitor, and acts as an appetite suppressant. Risks of concomitant use with SSRIs and SNRIs include serotonin syndrome, which can manifest with confusion, altered consciousness, sweating, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, dilated pupils, and required urgent medical intervention. Sibutramine has been withdrawn from the UK and many other countries.

questions.question_text: Which receptor blockade leads to this kind of effect?
questions.explanation:
Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant that acts as a serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. Its blockade of alpha adrenergic 1 receptor can cause dizziness, sedation, and hypotension. Sedative effects and weight gain can occur due to antihistaminic properties. Anticholinergic activity can cause sedative effects, dry mouth, constipation, and blurred vision.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 25-26.

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes the mechanism of action of Pregabalin?

options.text: Has a mechanism of action identical to GABA

questions.explanation:
Pregabalin is a leucine analog and is transported both into the blood from the gut and also across the blood-brain barrier into the brain by the system L transport system (a sodium-dependent transporter) as well as by additional sodium-dependent amino acid transporter systems. Pregabalin binds to the alpha 2 delta subunit of voltage-sensitive calcium channels. This closes N and P/Q presynaptic calcium channels, diminishing excessive neuronal activity and neurotransmitter release. Although structurally related to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), it has no known direct actions on GABA or its receptors.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 647.

questions.question_text: Blocking dopamine in which of the following pathways would result in hyperprolactinaemia?
questions.explanation:
The dopamine neurons that project from hypothalamus to anterior pituitary gland are known as the tuberoinfundibular dopamine pathway. Normally, these neurons are tonically active and inhibit prolactin release. In the postpartum state, however, the activity of these dopamine neurons is decreased. Prolactin levels can therefore rise during breast feeding so that lactation will occur. If the functioning of the tuberoinfundibular dopamine neurons is disrupted by lesions or drugs, prolactin levels can also rise.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 85.

questions.question_text: Zopiclone acts on which receptor site?
questions.explanation:
Z drugs bind to benzodiazepine-sensitive GABA-A receptors. A different nomenclature (omega system) denotes the specific sites of GABA-A receptors where these ‘Z’ drugs act as omega-1 receptors. Conventional benzodiazepines interact at both ω1 and ω2 sites, the latter likely contributing to side effects.
Zolpidem and zaleplon bind selectively to alpha-1 subunits of these sites. By contrast, benzodiazepines and zopiclone/eszopiclone bind to four alpha subunits (alpha-1, alpha-2, alpha-3, and alpha-5). The functional significance of alpha-1 selectivity is not yet proven, but may contribute to lower risk of tolerance and dependence. The alpha-1 subtype is known to be critical for producing sedation and thus is targeted by every effective GABA-A PAM (positive allosteric modulator) hypnotic, both benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 422-423.
Madari S, Golebiowski R, Mansukhani MP, Kolla BP. Pharmacological management of insomnia. Neurotherapeutics. 2021 Jan;18(1):44-52.

questions.question_text: Mr. Zane is a 60-year-old man who is on warfarin following a DVT. Which of the following medications would be the most important for him to avoid?
questions.explanation:
St. John’s wort (SJW) is a potent inducer of intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2E1, and intestinal p-glycoprotein. Hyperforin is responsible for this effect. The hyperforin content of SJW preparations varies 50-fold, which will result in a different propensity for drug interactions between brands. Studies have shown that SJW significantly reduces plasma concentrations of warfarin, hormonal contraceptives, digoxin, and indinavir (used in the treatment of HIV).
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 418.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is considered to be the most teratogenic?
questions.explanation:
Valproate is associated with strong evidence for increased risk of congenital and major congenital malformations (as many as 11% of exposed children); cleft lip and/or palate, neural tube defects (risk of spina bifida 1-2%), congenital heart anomalies, radial ray defects, ophthalmological and genitourinary anomalies; developmental delay (delayed walking and talking, memory problems, difficulty with speech and language), low IQ, and autism. This risk increases with increasing doses of valproic acid, especially when the dose is more than 1gm/day.
Ref: McAllister-Williams RH et al. British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus guidance on the use of psychotropic medication preconception, in pregnancy and postpartum 2017. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2017 May;31(5):519-52.
National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. Antenatal and postnatal mental health: clinical management and service guide. Updated edition 2020.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 690-691.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a medication that would best fit this description?
questions.explanation:
Naltrexone has been found by NICE to be a cost-effective treatment strategy in aiding abstinence from opioid misuse for those who prefer an abstinence programme (rather than substitute prescribing of methadone or buprenorphine), are fully informed of potential risks and benefits, are highly motivated to remain on treatment, and have a partner supporting concordance. It hasthe propensity to cause a severe withdrawal reaction from opioids. A test dose of naloxone, which has a much shorter half-life than naltrexone, may be given prior to starting naltrexone treatment; any withdrawal symptoms precipitated will be of shorter duration than if precipitated by naltrexone. Discontinuation may be associated with an increase in inadvertent overdose from illicit opioids, making supervision of administration and careful choice of who is prescribed it (abstinence-focused and motivated) very important. People taking naltrexone often experience adverse effects of unease (dysphoria), depression and insomnia, which can lead to relapse to illicit opioid use or failure to continue treatment.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 496.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neurotransmitters is primarily released from the medial and dorsal raphe nucleus?
questions.explanation:
Serotonin has both ascending and descending projections. Ascending serotonergic projections originate mainly in the raphe nucleus in the brainstem. These ascending projections may regulate mood, anxiety, sleep, and other functions. Descending serotonergic projections extend down the brainstem and through the spinal cord. They may regulate pain.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 279.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants will you avoid prescribing?
questions.explanation:
Fluoxetine may displace highly protein-bound drugs like warfarin. Fluoxetine carries a possible increased risk of bleeding, especially when combined with anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin, NSAIDs).
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 304.

questions.question_text: Which of the following psychotropic drugs is affected by acetylator (slow/fast) status?
questions.explanation:
Acetylation is a phase 2 nonmicrosomal conjugation reaction.
Drugs such as isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide, some sulfonamides, sulfasalazine, nitrazepam, and caffeine undergo acetylation.
The enzyme group responsible are the N-acetyltransferases.
There are two different isozymes in humans, encoded by the genes NAT1 and NAT2.
Based on the polymorphisms of NAT1 and NAT2, humans can be fast, intermediate, or slow acetylators.
60% of Caucasians and 10% to 20% of Asians are slow acetylators.
Slow acetylation contributes to prolonged half-life of the drug. This increases the risk of side effects such as peripheral neuropathy
(isoniazid), lupus syndrome (hydralazine and procainamaide), allergic reactions and hemolysis (sulfonamides), drowsiness, hangover
(nitrazepam), and gastrointestinal effects (sulfasalazine).
Ref: Kant A, Bilmen J, Hopkins PM. Adverse drug reactions. In Pharmacology and Physiology for Anesthesia 2019 Jan 1 (pp. 130-143).
Elsevier.

questions.explanation:
SSRI discontinuation symptoms may include flu-like symptoms, ‘shock-like’ sensations, dizziness (most common), insomnia, excessive dreaming, irritability, weakness, lethargy/fatigue, GI symptoms, and tearfulness. The onset of symptoms is usually within days (or 3-5 drug half-lives) of stopping treatment.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 143.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medication could decrease the effectiveness of the contraception?
questions.explanation:
Psychiatric drugs that are CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. carbamazepine, St John’s Wort, phenytoin, topiramate) reduce the bioavailability and hence contraceptive efficacy of combined hormonal contraceptives, the progesterone-only pill, and the subdermal implant both during use and for up to 28 days after stopping enzyme-inducer treatment. Thus, patients on enzyme inducers should be encouraged to use intrauterine contraception or injectables.
Ref: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 314.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 855.

questions.question_text: Which one of the above drugs would lead you to send him for an urgent INR?
questions.explanation:
St. John’s wort (SJW) is a potent inducer of intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2E1, and intestinal p-glycoprotein. Hyperforin is responsible for this effect. The hyperforin content of SJW preparations varies 50-fold, which will result in a different propensity for drug interactions between brands. Studies have shown that SJW significantly reduces plasma concentrations of warfarin, hormonal contraceptives, digoxin, and indinavir (used in the treatment of HIV).
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 418.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with respect to first-order elimination kinetics?

options.text: Constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit of time
Very few drugs undergo first order metabolism
Steady state concentration of the drug is doubled by doubling the administration rate
Clearance depends on concentration of the drug in plasma
Most commonly seen when metabolic enzymes are saturated

correct_answer.text: Steady state concentration of the drug is doubled by doubling the administration rate

correct_answers.text: Steady state concentration of the drug is doubled by doubling the administration rate

questions.explanation:
Constant fraction, not amount is eliminated per unit time if a drug undergoes first order elimination. Hence, clearance is independent of drug concentration in plasma. Doubling the administration rate will double the steady-state plasma concentration.
Ref: Laracuente ML, Marina HY, McHugh KJ. Zero-order drug delivery: State of the art and future prospects. Journal of Controlled Release. 2020 Nov 10;327:834-56.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about protein binding is incorrect?

options.text: Tissue binding of a drug cannot be directly measured
The distribution of a drug is not affected by the degree of protein binding
Plasma protein binding is usually reversible
Pregnancy can affect protein binding of drugs
Displacement bound fraction of a drug from plasma proteins may be a basis of drug interactions.

correct_answer.text: The distribution of a drug is not affected by the degree of protein binding

correct_answers.text: The distribution of a drug is not affected by the degree of protein binding

questions.explanation: The distribution of a drug depends on how protein bound it is. When in the blood, many drugs are bound to circulating plasma proteins, predominantly albumin but also globulins and glycoproteins. It is the unbound fraction of the drug (free fraction) that can be active i.e., bind to receptors, pass across blood brain barrier, etc. Therefore, changes in protein binding can have profound effects on the availability of the drugs. Most psychotropic drugs are basic, and they may bind to, for example, alpha-1 acid glycoprotein and lipoproteins. Plasma protein binding is usually reversible (not covalent).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following conditions is not considered to be a tauopathy?
questions.explanation:
Tauopathies including but not limited to Alzheimer disease, some frontotemporal dementias (e.g. Pick disease), corticobasal degeneration, progressive supranuclear palsy, and chronic traumatic encephalopathy, are progressive neurodegenerative disorders that are pathologically defined by tau-positive deposits in the brain.
Ref: Orr ME et al. A brief overview of tauopathy: causes, consequences, and therapeutic strategies. Trends in pharmacological sciences. 2017 Jul 1;38(7):637-48.

questions.question_text: In which of the following areas is the causative lesion most likely to be present?
questions.explanation: In pontine stroke, patients often experience ipsilateral facial palsy and contralateral limb paresis. In midbrain strokes, patients often experience contralateral facial and limb paresis but ipsilateral cranial nerve III palsy.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following neurological conditions has not been associated with REM sleep behaviour disorder?
questions.explanation: Alpha-synuclein pathology, as seen in Parkinson disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), is the most common underlying cause of RBD (REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder). Less commonly, RBD occurs in non-synuclein neurodegenerative disorders such as progressive supranuclear palsy, frontotemporal dementia, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Alzheimer disease, spinal cerebellar ataxia type 3, Huntington disease, and myotonic dystrophy type. Mononeuritis multiplex has not been associated with this illness. (Ref: Chan PC, Lee HH, Hong CT, Hu CJ, Wu D. REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) in Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB). Behavioural Neurology. 2018)

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests would be most useful to clarify the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An MRI head to check for intracranial complications of the initial injury would be the most sensible approach. The Wisconsin card test tests an individual's ability to “set shift" between one task and another. The International personality disorder examination, Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory and Myers-Briggs Personality Inventory are unlikely to be appropriate for an individual with a brain injury and declining cognition.

questions.question_text: A lesion in which of the following areas is most likely to lead to this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Neglect syndromes are characterised by failure to detect visual or tactile stimuli or to move the limb in the contralateral hemispace. They are most associated with right hemisphere damage in the parietal region. The right parietal lobe is non-dominant in most individuals.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 49.

questions.question_text: Sleep terrors most commonly occur during which of the following stages of sleep?
questions.explanation:
Sleep terrors are recurrent episodes of abrupt awakening from sleep characterised by a panicky scream, with intense fear and autonomic arousal. The individual usually has no recall of the details of the event and is unresponsive to stimuli (e.g conversation) during the episode. Autonomic hyperactivity is manifested by tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, flushed face, dilated pupils, agitation, tremulousness, and increased muscle tone. A typical episode lasts no more than a few minutes, but may be protracted, lasting up to an hour.
Sleep terrors occur during the first third of the night, during slow-wave stage 3 of NREM sleep. NREM is classified as stages 1 to 3 with increasing amplitude and decreasing frequency of EEG activity. Stage 3 (previously split as 3 & 4) constitutes slow wave sleep (SWS). SWS dominates initial part of the sleep.
Ref: Leung AK et al. Sleep terrors: an updated review. Current pediatric reviews. 2020 Aug 1;16(3):176-82.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 462.

questions.question_text: Which of the following immunostaining findings are associated with classical neurofibrillary tangles?
questions.explanation:
Neurofibrillary tangles are intracellular inclusion bodies, primarily containing tau as well as other proteins. Tau is a microtubule-binding protein, but in tangles, it has separated from the microtubules and is hyperphosphorylated at a variety of serine and threonine residues. Tangles may be detected by immunostaining for tau protein, as well as silver impregnation techniques such as Bielschowsky or Gallyas stains. Tangles are particularly well demonstrated by tau immunocytochemistry, which is now used routinely in diagnostic work. Neurofibrillary tangles may on occasion also be immunoreactive for ubiquitin and p62.
Ref: Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6th Edition. 2019. pp. 5, 189.

questions.question_text: Which of the following brain areas tend to be larger in patients with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Neuropathology in schizophrenia includes larger ventricles, decreases in gray matter and whole-brain volume, white matter anisotropy, reduced prefrontal lobe volume, and reduced volume of the medial temporal lobes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following brain regions plays an important role in the memory of emotionally salient events?
questions.explanation:
The amygdala is an almond-shaped brain structure in the limbic system at the base of the inside of each temporal lobe, contiguous with the olfactory cortex, controlling the experience and expression of emotion and involved in motivation, aggression, feeding, and (through its links with the hippocampus) long-term memory. Electrical stimulation of this area usually produces an intense emotion of fear.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Damage to which part of the brain can result in Anton's syndrome?
questions.explanation: Anton–Babinski syndrome, also known as visual anosognosia, is a rare symptom of brain damage occurring in the occipital lobe. Those who suffer from it are "cortically blind", but insist that they are capable of seeing despite evidence to the contrary. Sufferers dismiss evidence of their condition and employ confabulation to fill in the missing sensory input.

questions.question_text: The form of Down syndrome which is as likely to have come from the father's as that of mother's chromosome is:
questions.explanation:
Partial or complete trisomy 21 (that is, the presence of part of or a complete supernumerary chromosome 21) is the genomic cause of Down syndrome (DS). Most cases of DS are not inherited. However, people with translocation DS can inherit the condition from an unaffected parent (either paternal or maternal). Translocation accounts for trisomy 21 in ~5% of affected individuals, usually t(14;21) or t(21;21). In translocation, a fusion occurs, of two chromosomes, resulting in a total of 46 chromosomes, despite the presence of an extra chromosome 21. This is usually inherited, and the translocated chromosome may be found in unaffected parents and siblings. Asymptomatic carriers have only 45 chromosomes.
A free trisomy 21 is present in 95% of individuals with DS and results from an error in maternal meiosis I (~66%) or meiosis II (~21%); paternal meiosis I (~3%) or meiosis II (~5%); or mitosis, after the formation of the zygote (5%). Advanced maternal age has been associated with chromosome 21 segregation errors in both maternal meiosis I and meiosis II. Mosaicism for trisomy 21 is not inherited and occurs in ~2% of individuals with DS.
Ref: Antonarakis SE et al. Down syndrome. Nature Reviews Disease Primers. 2020 Feb 6;6(1):1-20.

questions.question_text: Smooth pursuit eye tracking dysfunction is proposed as a strong endophenotype marker for which of the following group of disorders?
questions.explanation:
The inability to follow a moving visual target accurately is the defining basis for the disorders of smooth visual pursuit and disinhibition of saccadic eye movements seen in patients with schizophrenia. Eye movement dysfunction may be a trait marker for schizophrenia; it is independent of drug treatment and clinical state and also occurs in first-degree relatives of probands with schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following personality disorders has the strongest support for a genetic contribution?
questions.explanation:
Schizotypal disorder is currently viewed as representing ‘partial expression’ of the schizophrenia phenotype. Schizophrenia twin studies show an increased risk of schizotypy in the unaffected twin, schizotypy is more common in first-degree relatives of schizophrenic subjects than the general population, and relatives of schizotypal subjects show an increased risk of schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 228-229.

questions.question_text: Which of the following behaviours is consistent with this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an extremely rare recessive condition due to a mutation in the HGPRT gene on the short arm of the X chromosome. Deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine phosphoribosyl transferase leads to build of uric acid in the body fluids; partial HGPRT deficiency results in gout. Early features include hypotonia and delayed motor milestones; extra pyramidal signs such as spasticity and choreo-athetoid movements develop at about 9 months; hyperreflexia and clonus appear at about 1 year. Severe compulsive self-mutilation usually presents between the ages of 2-3; biting of the lips, inside of mouth, fingers.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 816.

questions.question_text: Trinucleotide repeat expansions in DNA can be detected using
questions.explanation:
Developed by and named after Edward Southern, a Southern blot is used to identify if a known DNA sequence is present in a sample by using a specific probe to identify the sequence in a large mixture of other DNA fragments. As trinucleotide repeats are DNA abnormalities, the Southern blot can be used to detect them.

questions.question_text: Which of the following cells can be described as macrophages of the central nervous system?
questions.explanation:
There are three types of glial cells. The most common are the astrocytes, which have several functions, including nutrition of neurons, deactivation of some neurotransmitters, and integration with the blood-brain barrier. Mature astrocytes also express some genes enriched in cell progenitors, suggesting they can retain proliferative potential. Theoligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and the Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system wrap their processed around neuronal axons, resulting in myelin sheaths that facilitate the conduction of electrical signals. The third type of glial cells, the microglia, which are derived from macrophages, are involved in removing cellular debris following neuronal death. The functions of microglia in the non-diseased brain probably include a role in synaptic maintenance.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 924.

questions.question_text: The part of the brain involved in reward processing is
questions.explanation:
The midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA) lies medial to the substantia nigra and contains dopaminergic neurons that give rise to the mesocorticolimbic dopamine system. These neurons send ascending projections that innervate limbic structures, such as the nucleus accumbens and amygdala; the mesoaccumbens pathway is a central element in the neural representation of reward.
The amygdala - an almond-shaped group of nuclei at the heart of the telencephalon - has been associated with a range of cognitive functions. Most prior work on amygdala function emphasized its role in negative emotions, such as fear, and in linking negative emotions with other aspects of cognition, such as learning and memory. However, recent evidence supports a role for the amygdala in processing positive emotions as well as negative ones, including learning about the beneficial biological value of stimuli. Indeed, the amygdala's role in stimulus-reward learning might be just as important as its role in processing negative affect and fear conditioning. In particular, neurons in this region appear to be sensitive to background reward (contingency) and code reward amount and timing, and signal economic decision processes. Primate research also indicates that a mygdala may simulate economic decisions of social partners.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 955.
Grabenhorst F, Schultz W. Functions of primate amygdala neurons in economic decisions and social decision simulation. Behavioural Brain Research. 2021 Jul 9;409:113318.
